# Research Compendia with rrtools {#sec-rrtools} A collaborator clones your repository, runs the analysis script, and gets a p-value of 0.06 where your draft reports 0.04. Nothing errors. Over two days the two of you find three differences: her R packages are a year newer than yours, the cleaned dataset in the repository was produced by a version of the cleaning script you have since edited, and one exclusion was made by hand in a spreadsheet that never entered the repository. Each difference is a piece of the study that did not travel with the code. A research compendium is the arrangement in which everything needed to produce the paper, from the raw data to the environment, lives in one directory with a layout a stranger can read, so that the collaborator's rerun either matches or tells you why not. ::: {.bookepigraph} ```{=latex} \begin{flushright}\small ``` *We introduce the concept of a compendium as both a container for the different elements that make up the document and its computations, and as a means for distributing, managing and updating the collection.* [Robert Gentleman and Duncan Temple Lang]{.smallcaps}, *Statistical Analyses and Reproducible Research* (2007) ```{=latex} \end{flushright} ``` ::: ::: {.column-margin} ![Robert Gentleman, co-creator of R and, with Duncan Temple Lang, author of the 2007 paper that introduced the research compendium this chapter builds on. Photograph by the R Consortium, [CC BY 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/), via Wikimedia Commons.](images/portraits/gentleman.jpg){fig-alt='Portrait photograph of Robert Gentleman.'} ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Where this chapter sits: the compendium is what you share, the whole pipeline from raw data to report packaged so that someone else can rerun it.](07-rrtools_files/figure-pdf/fig-rrtools-pipeline-1.pdf){#fig-rrtools-pipeline fig-align='center' fig-alt='Diagram of the analysis pipeline: six stages in order (Plan, Acquire, Wrangle, Analyze, Report, Share) above two bands that run under every stage (Version control and Environment). Highlighted for this chapter: Share.' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note title='In this chapter'} **Reading time.** About 20 minutes. **You'll need.** @sec-git-solo for commits and tags, and @sec-quarto for the paper. Two of the five pillars are taught in their own chapters, @sec-renv and @sec-docker; this chapter shows where they sit. The executed examples use base R and `purrr`: ```r library(purrr) ``` **You'll be able to.** - Name the five pillars of a compendium and, for a given repository, say which are missing and what failure each gap allows. - Place each file of a project in the conventional layout, and protect the raw data with a checksum manifest. - Scaffold a compendium with `rrtools` or a Quarto project, and write the paper inside it. - Verify a compendium by rebuilding it from a fresh clone. **Outline.** - [What a research compendium is](#sec-rrtools-what) - [The five pillars](#sec-rrtools-pillars) - [Where files go](#sec-rrtools-layout) - [Scaffolding a compendium](#sec-rrtools-scaffold) - [The paper inside the compendium](#sec-rrtools-paper) - [Building and sharing](#sec-rrtools-build) - [Worked example: a small compendium](#sec-rrtools-worked) ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Skip ahead?'} If these answers come quickly, skip to the next chapter. The answers are in @sec-quiz-answers-07. 1. What is a 'research compendium' as described by Marwick, Boettiger, and Mullen (2018) [@marwick2018packaging]? 2. What are the three essential components of an `rrtools` compendium? 3. How does an `rrtools` compendium differ from a regular R package? ::: ## What a research compendium is {#sec-rrtools-what} A paper without its compendium is a description of an analysis; a compendium without a paper is code. Together they are a study artifact that survives the loss of any individual file, and of any individual person. Gentleman and Temple Lang [-@gentleman2007statistical] introduced the term, and Marwick, Boettiger, and Mullen [-@marwick2018packaging] gave the working definition this book uses, which has three criteria: | Criterion | What it requires | What fails without it | |---|---|---| | Single directory | Code, data, environment, and narrative together | A step lives elsewhere (a spreadsheet, a laptop), as the hand exclusion in the opening did | | Computable | Another user can rerun the analysis with reasonable effort | The paper can be read but not checked | | Self-describing | The layout follows a convention a stranger knows | Every file is a hunt, for the stranger and for you in eighteen months | : The three criteria for a research compendium. {#tbl-rrtools-criteria} The argument for convention is practical. A directory organized to your own logic is navigable by you and by nobody else, and 'nobody else' includes the version of you that returns after eighteen months. A compendium that follows a recognized layout can be opened by a stranger who has seen one before: they will know where the paper is, where the raw data are, and which directory holds things that were derived rather than given. The specific convention matters much less than having one at all. R packages already have a convention every R user knows (`DESCRIPTION`, `R/`, `man/`), which satisfies the third criterion and part of the first. What a package lacks is a study: data and a paper. The `rrtools` package [@marwick2018rrtools] supplies one convention that adds them, and @fig-compendium-anatomy shows the result. ```{mermaid} %%| echo: false %%| label: fig-compendium-anatomy %%| fig-alt: "Flowchart. A research compendium branches into three %%| components: a package backbone of DESCRIPTION, R/ and man/; %%| an analysis directory holding data, paper and figures; and a %%| Dockerfile with renv.lock. Each leads in turn to the property %%| it supplies: self-describing so a stranger can navigate it, a %%| single directory holding code, data and narrative together, %%| and computable so another user can re-run it." %%| fig-cap: "What a compendium is made of. The package backbone %%| supplies convention and dependency declaration; the analysis %%| directory supplies the study; the Dockerfile supplies the %%| environment. Remove any of the three and the reader loses %%| navigability, content, or the ability to run it." flowchart TD C["Research compendium"] C --> P["Package backbone
DESCRIPTION, R/, man/
convention and dependencies"] C --> A["analysis/
data/, paper/, figures/
the study itself"] C --> D["Dockerfile + renv.lock
the environment"] P --> N["self-describing
a stranger can navigate it"] A --> S["single directory
code, data, narrative together"] D --> R["computable
another user can re-run it"] ``` ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** Why does `rrtools` reuse the R package structure instead of inventing a new layout? **Answer.** Three practical reasons. The package structure is the only widely recognized layout in the R ecosystem, so the compendium is navigable for free. The package gives dependency declaration: `DESCRIPTION` lists what the code needs, and `renv` (@sec-renv) pins the versions. And it gives function management: helpers in `R/` are documented, tested, and loadable into the analysis. The cost is a few package files that are not used as a package (no CRAN, the Comprehensive R Archive Network, submission, no users importing it), which is small against the structural payoff. ::: ## The five pillars {#sec-rrtools-pillars} The three criteria say what a compendium must achieve. The five pillars say what it must contain to achieve them. The book uses the R tools for each, but the pillars are roles, and every language has a tool for each role: | Pillar | What it pins | In this book | Elsewhere | Without it, the opening's rerun differs because | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1. Environment beneath R | OS, system libraries, the R build | `Dockerfile` (@sec-docker) | Apptainer definition, Nix | A system library or R version changed | | 2. Package versions | Every R package, exactly | `renv.lock` (@sec-renv) | `uv.lock`, conda `environment.yml` | Her packages were a year newer | | 3. Project activation | That the project uses its own library | `.Rprofile` (@sec-renv) | A virtual-environment activation script | The lockfile exists but her session ignored it | | 4. Source code | Every step, from raw data to every number | `R/` and `analysis/` in Git (@sec-git-solo) | Any version-controlled scripts | A hand step or an edited script is not in the history | | 5. Data | The raw inputs, unchanged, or the documented way to get them | `analysis/data/raw_data/` with a checksum manifest | A DOI'd deposit with access instructions | A stale derived file stood in for the raw data | : The five pillars of a compendium. Each is necessary; none is sufficient. {#tbl-rrtools-pillars} The opening's three causes map onto pillars 2, 4, and 5. The remedy for each is not care but a file: a lockfile, a script for every step, and raw data that the code reads and never writes. Some frameworks automate the pillars; `zzcollab` (@sec-zzcollab) is one, and it scaffolds and audits all five. The audit itself needs nothing but the file system. The chunk below builds a toy compendium in a temporary directory, with two of the HF-HOME raw files, and checks which pillars are present. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(purrr) comp <- file.path(tempdir(), 'readmissions') layout <- c('R', 'analysis/data/raw_data', 'analysis/data/derived_data', 'analysis/paper', 'analysis/figures') walk(file.path(comp, layout), dir.create, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE) hf_dir <- file.path('..', 'data', 'raw_data', 'hfhome') raw_dir <- file.path(comp, 'analysis', 'data', 'raw_data') file.copy(file.path(hf_dir, c('randomization.csv', 'outcomes.csv')), raw_dir, overwrite = TRUE) #> [1] TRUE TRUE writeLines(c('Package: readmissions', 'Version: 0.0.1'), file.path(comp, 'DESCRIPTION')) writeLines(c('---', 'title: "Draft"', '---'), file.path(comp, 'analysis', 'paper', 'paper.qmd')) pillars <- data.frame( pillar = c('1. Environment', '2. Package versions', '3. Activation', '4. Source code', '5. Data'), path = c('Dockerfile', 'renv.lock', '.Rprofile', '.git', 'analysis/data/raw_data/MANIFEST.md5') ) audit_pillars <- function(root) { transform(pillars, present = file.exists(file.path(root, path))) } audit_pillars(comp) #> pillar path present #> 1 1. Environment Dockerfile FALSE #> 2 2. Package versions renv.lock FALSE #> 3 3. Activation .Rprofile FALSE #> 4 4. Source code .git FALSE #> 5 5. Data analysis/data/raw_data/MANIFEST.md5 FALSE ``` ::: The toy has a layout and data but none of the five pillars in recorded form: no environment specification, no lockfile, no activation, no Git history, and no record of what the raw data were. This is a structural check, in the sense of @sec-testing: a file that exists can still be wrong. It finds what is missing, and it cannot tell you that what is present works. The test that does is the rebuild from a fresh clone in @sec-rrtools-build. ::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'} Run the same audit on your own project, and treat every `FALSE` as a gap to close or a decision to document in the README (for example, raw data that cannot be shared, with the access path in its place): ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} audit_pillars('.') ``` ::: For a project under Git, `git ls-files Dockerfile renv.lock .Rprofile` confirms that the files are committed, not merely present on your disk. ::: ### Exercises 1. A repository contains `analysis.R`, `clean.R`, `data.csv` (described in the README as 'cleaned'), `renv.lock`, and a README that says 'run analysis.R in RStudio'. Which pillars are present, which are missing, and what would a collaborator's rerun be unable to establish? ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} Present: package versions (`renv.lock`) and source code, assuming the repository is under Git. Missing: the environment beneath R (no Dockerfile, so R and system libraries are whatever the collaborator has), activation (no `.Rprofile`, so the lockfile is ignored unless she restores it by hand), and the raw data. The data pillar is the serious gap: `data.csv` is derived, so a rerun can check `analysis.R` against it but can never check `clean.R`, and any hand step between the raw export and `data.csv` is invisible. Add the raw export (or its access path), make `clean.R` read it and write to `derived_data/`, and record a checksum manifest. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** Your compendium has a `renv.lock` and a Dockerfile. A colleague argues that the lockfile is redundant, because the image already contains the packages. Is it? **Answer.** No. The image contains the packages that were current when it was built, and a rebuild months later installs whatever is current then, unless the lockfile pins them; the Dockerfile's restore step reads the lockfile for exactly that reason. The pillars are a stack, not a menu: the Dockerfile pins what is beneath R, and the lockfile pins what is above it. ::: ## Where files go {#sec-rrtools-layout} ### The layout `rrtools` produces the layout below; most compendium conventions differ from it only in names. ``` readmissions/ ├── DESCRIPTION ├── NAMESPACE ├── R/ # reusable functions ├── man/ ├── analysis/ │ ├── data/ │ │ ├── raw_data/ │ │ └── derived_data/ │ ├── figures/ │ ├── paper/ │ │ ├── paper.qmd │ │ └── references.bib │ └── supplementary-materials/ ├── Dockerfile ├── .github/ │ └── workflows/ ├── README.qmd ├── README.md └── readmissions.Rproj ``` | Path | Holds | Commit it? | |---|---|---| | `R/` | Reusable functions: cleaning helpers, plotting wrappers, model utilities, documented with roxygen | Yes | | `analysis/data/raw_data/` | The data exactly as received, never edited | If small and unrestricted; otherwise document the access path | | `analysis/data/derived_data/` | Everything the scripts produce from the raw data | Optional: commit when small and the analysis is archived | | `analysis/paper/paper.qmd` | The manuscript, with the code that produces its numbers | Yes | | `analysis/figures/` | Figures the analysis writes | Usually not; the code that makes them is committed | | `analysis/supplementary-materials/` | Appendix tables, sensitivity analyses | Yes | | `README.qmd` | What the project is, how to build it in one command, where the paper and data are, how to cite it | Yes | : Where each file goes. {#tbl-rrtools-layout} The README is the entry point, not the documentation: it says what the project is, how to rebuild it, and where things are. Long technical notes live elsewhere. ### Raw data are read-only Raw and derived data live in separate directories because raw data are evidence and derived data are a build product. Writing a cleaned table back over the input destroys the only copy of what you were given, and version control does not recover a file that was overwritten before it was ever committed. Treat `raw_data/` as read-only, by convention if your file system will not enforce it, and make the convention checkable: record a checksum of every raw file when it arrives. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} raw_files <- list.files(raw_dir, pattern = '\\.csv$') sums <- tools::md5sum(file.path(raw_dir, raw_files)) writeLines(paste0(sums, ' ', raw_files), file.path(raw_dir, 'MANIFEST.md5')) readLines(file.path(raw_dir, 'MANIFEST.md5')) #> [1] "7df9965b772962e3a709b826790eea9b outcomes.csv" #> [2] "527ded58d20ec4687aa5068c7ff30da1 randomization.csv" check_raw <- function(raw_dir) { lines <- readLines(file.path(raw_dir, 'MANIFEST.md5')) recorded <- setNames(sub(' .*$', '', lines), sub('^\\S+ ', '', lines)) current <- tools::md5sum(file.path(raw_dir, names(recorded))) changed <- names(recorded)[unname(current) != recorded] if (length(changed) > 0) { stop('raw data changed since the manifest: ', paste(changed, collapse = ', '), call. = FALSE) } invisible(TRUE) } check_raw(raw_dir) ``` ::: The manifest uses the format of the `md5sum` command, so `md5sum -c MANIFEST.md5` checks it from the shell as well (on Linux, or on macOS with the GNU coreutils installed). MD5 is adequate for detecting accidental change, which is the job here; it is not a defense against deliberate tampering. ::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'} **A 'quick fix' saved over the raw export leaves no trace in the data.** Exclude a few patients by hand and save the file in place, and every later run reads the edited file as if it were what the site sent: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} outcomes_path <- file.path(raw_dir, 'outcomes.csv') outcomes <- read.csv(outcomes_path, colClasses = c(patient_id = 'character')) write.csv(outcomes[-(1:3), ], outcomes_path, row.names = FALSE) check_raw(raw_dir) #> Error: #> ! raw data changed since the manifest: outcomes.csv ``` ::: The analysis would have run, on 2,429 patients instead of 2,432, with no error. The manifest makes it loud. Exclusions belong in code, in `derived_data/`, where they are counted and reviewed. ::: ### Exercises 2. Assign each file from a messy project to the layout of @tbl-rrtools-layout: `helpers.R` (three functions used by two scripts), `crf_export_2025-06-01.csv` (from the data center), `analytic.rds` (written by `clean.R`), `fig2.png`, `notes.txt` (a dated log of decisions), `clean.R`, and `manuscript.qmd`. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} | File | Goes to | Why | |---|---|---| | `helpers.R` | `R/` | Reused by more than one script | | `crf_export_2025-06-01.csv` | `analysis/data/raw_data/` | Received, not produced; add it to the manifest | | `analytic.rds` | `analysis/data/derived_data/` | Produced by a script; regenerable | | `fig2.png` | `analysis/figures/` (usually untracked) | Produced by code | | `notes.txt` | Top level or `analysis/` as a decision log | Not data and not code; keep it with the project and in Git | | `clean.R` | `analysis/` (scripts) | Study-specific code that turns raw into derived data | | `manuscript.qmd` | `analysis/paper/paper.qmd` | The manuscript | The judgment calls are `notes.txt`, which fits no category and should not be forced into one, and `clean.R`, which some conventions put in `analysis/scripts/`. What matters is that a stranger can predict the location. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** Your cleaning script reads `analysis/data/raw_data/visits.csv` and produces a tidy analytic table. Where does the output go, and should it be committed? **Answer.** It goes in `analysis/data/derived_data/`, and whether to commit it is a trade-off, not a rule. Against committing: it is reproducible from the raw data and the script, so storing it duplicates information and adds a binary that changes on every run. For committing: it lets a reader check your numbers without installing your environment, and it fixes what the analysis actually used, which matters if the cleaning script is later corrected. The usual resolution is to commit derived data when it is small and the analysis is being archived, and to leave it untracked during development. What is not defensible is committing derived data and *not* the script that made it, which is the arrangement that looks tidiest and explains least, and the one behind the opening's stale dataset. ::: ## Scaffolding a compendium {#sec-rrtools-scaffold} ### With `rrtools` The calls below are display-only, because they create a project and open it as a new RStudio session: ```r # install install.packages("remotes") remotes::install_github("benmarwick/rrtools") # create a new compendium rrtools::use_compendium("~/research/readmissions") # (this also runs usethis::create_package internally) # add the analysis directories rrtools::use_analysis() # add a Dockerfile and, by default, a GitHub Actions # workflow that renders the paper inside it rrtools::use_dockerfile() # add a README.qmd rrtools::use_readme_qmd() ``` `rrtools::use_dockerfile()` writes its own Dockerfile, based on `rocker/verse`. This book replaces it with the canonical Dockerfile in @sec-rrtools-build, so that this chapter, @sec-renv, and @sec-docker describe one file rather than several. ### Other conventions `rrtools` is one convention among several, and the right one depends on the project's shape and the team's habits: | Convention | Shape | Use when | |---|---|---| | `rrtools` | R package plus `analysis/` | A paper with reusable R code; the default for a biostatistical paper | | Quarto manuscript project | A Quarto project whose output is an article | A paper-first project without a package backbone | | Quarto book | A Quarto project with chapters | Book-length output, such as this practicum | | A framework such as `zzcollab` (@sec-zzcollab) | Scaffolds all five pillars and audits them | You want the pillars generated and checked for you | | The TIER Protocol (Teaching Integrity in Empirical Research) | A documented folder convention | Social-science collaborators who already use it | | Your group's template | Whatever the group agreed | Always, if one exists: consistency with colleagues beats any external default | : Compendium conventions. {#tbl-rrtools-conventions} Defaulting to `rrtools` is reasonable; defaulting to it without thought is not. ::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'} Use a model to propose a layout for an existing project, and apply the moves yourself. > **Context.** Below is the output of `git ls-files` for an R > analysis project, and the compendium layout I want (the table of > paths and contents). The working tree is clean and committed. > > **Constraints.** Propose only `git mv` commands. Do not move, > rename, or edit anything under `data/raw/`; raw files keep their > names and contents, and are moved, if at all, only into > `analysis/data/raw_data/` with a separate command I will run > myself. Delete nothing. Do not edit file contents. > > **Criteria.** Every file is assigned exactly once. List the > files that fit no category, with your reasoning, rather than > forcing them into one, and list every script whose file paths > will break after the moves. *Failure mode.* A model assigns every file somewhere, confidently, including logs and exploratory notebooks that fit nowhere, and proposes edits to paths inside scripts that silently change what they read. Raw files moved or renamed lose the link to their provenance. *Check.* After applying the moves, `git status` and `git diff -M --name-status HEAD` should show only renames (`R100`), no modifications or deletions; `md5sum -c MANIFEST.md5` in the raw-data directory should pass; and a fresh render should produce the same numbers. The prompt sends file names, not data (@sec-ai-governance). ::: ## The paper inside the compendium {#sec-rrtools-paper} `analysis/paper/paper.qmd` is the manuscript, written in Quarto (@sec-quarto): code chunks for the analyses, inline numbers, figure cross-references, and citations from `references.bib`. ````qmd --- title: "Effect of post-discharge home health visits on 30-day readmission" author: - name: A. Author - name: B. Coauthor format: pdf: default html: default bibliography: references.bib --- # Methods We analyzed `{{r}} nrow(d)` patients from the institutional EHR cohort. The primary outcome was 30-day all-cause readmission and the exposure was receipt of a home-health visit. We fit a multivariable logistic regression adjusting for age, sex, baseline ejection fraction, and discharge medications, in R [@rcore2024]. ```{{r}} #| label: fit-model #| echo: false fit <- glm(readmit ~ home_health + age + sex + ef + meds, family = binomial, data = d) ci <- exp(confint.default(fit)["home_health", ]) ``` The adjusted odds ratio for home-health-visit receipt was `{{r}} round(exp(coef(fit)["home_health"]), 2)` (95% CI `{{r}} round(ci[1], 2)` to `{{r}} round(ci[2], 2)`). ```` Every number in the methods and results comes from code, so a rerun on corrected data changes the prose with the tables. EHR here is the electronic health record; the example is an observational cohort, which is why the exposure is receipt of a visit and the estimate is adjusted. For journal-specific formatting in Quarto, use a Quarto journal extension where one exists for your journal. The `quarto-journals` collection on GitHub includes, for example, a template for JASA (the *Journal of the American Statistical Association*): ```bash quarto use template quarto-journals/jasa ``` The extension adds a format (here `jasa-pdf`) that you name under `format:` in `paper.qmd`. The older `rticles` package offers more journals, including *Statistics in Medicine*, *Biometrics*, and JASA (`rticles::journals()` lists them), but its templates are R Markdown output formats for an `.Rmd` file rendered with `rmarkdown::render()`, not Quarto formats; they cannot be named in the `format:` key of a `.qmd`. Neither collection has a template for every medical journal (there is none for NEJM or JAMA, for instance), and most of those journals accept a plain PDF or Word manuscript at first submission. ::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'} Render the paper in a fresh session and read the warnings, which are where unresolved citations and cross-references surface: ```bash quarto render analysis/paper/paper.qmd 2>&1 | grep -i warn ``` It should print nothing. A warning that a citation or a cross-reference cannot be resolved means the rendered paper shows a placeholder where a reference belongs. ::: ## Building and sharing {#sec-rrtools-build} A compendium is built in one of three ways: render the paper in RStudio while writing; source the analysis scripts in order after `devtools::load_all()` to regenerate cached results; or build the image, which is the only one that reproduces the environment as well as the results. The book's canonical Dockerfile, explained line by line in @sec-docker-canonical, sits at the compendium root: ```dockerfile # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1 FROM rocker/r-ver:4.4.0 ARG QUARTO_VERSION=1.6.40 RUN apt-get update \ && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \ ca-certificates curl \ libcurl4-openssl-dev libssl-dev libxml2-dev libuv1-dev \ && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* # rocker/r-ver ships R but not the Quarto CLI RUN arch="$(dpkg --print-architecture)" \ && curl -fsSL -o /tmp/quarto.deb \ "https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/releases/download/v${QUARTO_VERSION}/quarto-${QUARTO_VERSION}-linux-${arch}.deb" \ && dpkg -i /tmp/quarto.deb \ && rm /tmp/quarto.deb # outside /work, so a bind mount of the project cannot hide it ENV RENV_PATHS_LIBRARY=/opt/renv/library WORKDIR /work COPY renv.lock .Rprofile ./ COPY renv/activate.R renv/activate.R RUN R -q -e "renv::restore(prompt = FALSE)" COPY . . CMD ["quarto", "render", "analysis/paper/paper.qmd"] ``` From the compendium root (display-only): ```bash docker build --platform linux/amd64 -t readmissions:v1.0 . docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 \ -v "$(pwd)/analysis/paper:/work/analysis/paper" \ readmissions:v1.0 ``` The Dockerfile pins the R version, the system libraries, and (through `renv.lock`) the package versions, and the rendered paper appears in `analysis/paper/` on your machine. A reader with Docker can rebuild a very close copy of the environment that produced the paper; an exact copy needs the digest pin or archived image described in @sec-docker. Deposition is treated in full in @sec-federal. Its shape affects how you organize the directory, so it is worth knowing now: GitHub (or your institution's Git server) holds the working repository; an archive such as Zenodo holds a citable, DOI-bearing (digital object identifier) snapshot at submission, with the saved image; and restricted primary data go only where the data use agreement permits, often a controlled-access repository and sometimes nowhere, with the compendium documenting how to request them. ::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'} The test of a compendium is a rebuild by someone who is not you, from what is in the repository and nothing else. Simulate it (display-only): ```bash git clone https://github.com/you/readmissions.git /tmp/fresh cd /tmp/fresh docker build --platform linux/amd64 -t readmissions:check . docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 \ -v "$(pwd)/analysis/paper:/work/analysis/paper" readmissions:check ``` The paper must render, and its key numbers must match yours. A failure here names a file that lives only on your machine, which is the opening's problem found before your collaborator finds it. ::: ### Exercises 3. A colleague's compendium renders on her laptop and fails in the fresh-clone check with `cannot open file 'analysis/data/derived_data/analytic.rds'`. What is the likely cause, and what are the two acceptable fixes? ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} The paper reads a derived file that exists on her disk and is not in the repository, probably because `derived_data/` is listed in `.gitignore` and nothing in the build regenerates it. Either make the build produce it (the paper, or a script the Dockerfile's command runs, calls the cleaning code on the raw data), which is the better fix because it also tests the cleaning; or commit the derived file together with the script that made it, which is acceptable for an archived analysis. Committing it without the script is the arrangement the layout Check warned against. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** Why is the fresh clone the right test, rather than rendering the paper again on your own machine? **Answer.** Your machine has everything the repository forgot: the packages you installed, the derived files you never committed, the environment variables in your `.Renviron`. A rerun there passes whatever the compendium is missing. A fresh clone, built in a container, has only what the five pillars supply, so it is the first run that can fail for the reasons a collaborator's would. ::: ## Worked example: a small compendium {#sec-rrtools-worked} A simulation study set up as a compendium from scratch (display-only): ```r # scaffold; this opens the new compendium as its own # RStudio project, and every later call runs in that # session, whose working directory is the compendium rrtools::use_compendium("~/research/sim2026") rrtools::use_analysis() rrtools::use_readme_qmd() # the environment pillars: initialize renv, then replace # rrtools's Dockerfile with the canonical one renv::init() # add the simulation function usethis::use_r("simulate") # (write R/simulate.R with a documented function) devtools::document() # add the paper file.edit("analysis/paper/paper.qmd") # (write the manuscript using simulate() from the package) # render quarto::quarto_render("analysis/paper/paper.qmd") # version control usethis::use_git() usethis::use_github(private = TRUE) ``` Then snapshot, commit, and tag the milestone from the shell, in the compendium directory: ```bash Rscript -e 'renv::snapshot()' git add . git commit -m "Initial compendium" git tag -a v0.1-draft -m "Initial draft for PI review" ``` The compendium is now a self-contained directory with package-style code, a paper that uses the code, a lockfile and a Dockerfile that pin the environment, a Git history, and a tag at a meaningful milestone. The setup takes about thirty minutes. ::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'} Confirm that the pillars are committed and the tree is clean: ```bash git ls-files Dockerfile renv.lock .Rprofile analysis/paper/paper.qmd git status --short git tag -l 'v0.1*' ``` The first command should list all four files, the second should print nothing, and the third should print `v0.1-draft`. Then run the fresh-clone check of @sec-rrtools-build against the tag. ::: ## Rules of thumb 1. **Habit 1: the compendium is the unit.** Code, data, environment, and paper travel together in one directory with a convention a stranger knows; anything outside it is a step nobody can rerun. 2. **Habit 2: raw data are evidence; derived data are a build product.** Never write to `raw_data/`, record its checksums, and regenerate everything else from code. 3. **Habit 3: version control from day one.** Commit the pillars with the work that needs them, and tag what you submit; the fresh clone of that tag is the test. ## Cumulative practice 4. *Cumulative (uses @sec-git-solo and @sec-quarto).* Build a compendium for a small HF-HOME analysis: copy `randomization.csv` and `outcomes.csv` into `analysis/data/raw_data/` with a checksum manifest, write a `paper.qmd` that reports the 30-day event proportion in each arm with inline code, commit, and tag `v0.1`. Run `audit_pillars()` and the fresh-clone check, and record which pillars you still lack and why. 5. *On your own work (no key).* Convert a 'scripts and data' project of your own into a compendium. Document the location of every file and the reason for it, and record what the fresh-clone check found the first time you ran it. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} 4. The paper's numbers come from the raw files, never typed. A minimal computing chunk: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} rand <- read.csv(file.path(raw_dir, 'randomization.csv'), colClasses = c(patient_id = 'character')) outc <- read.csv(file.path(hf_dir, 'outcomes.csv'), colClasses = c(patient_id = 'character')) hf <- merge(rand[c('patient_id', 'arm')], outc[c('patient_id', 'event_30d')], by = 'patient_id') stopifnot(nrow(hf) == nrow(rand)) round(100 * tapply(hf$event_30d, hf$arm, mean, na.rm = TRUE), 1) #> Home health Usual care #> 21.1 23.7 ``` ::: The chunk reads `outcomes.csv` from the HF-HOME directory, because the Pitfall above edited the toy compendium's copy; in your compendium, both files come from `raw_data/`, and `check_raw()` runs first. Without a Dockerfile and a lockfile, the audit reports pillars 1 to 3 missing, and the fresh-clone check depends on whatever R the clone's machine has; the record should say so. ::: ## Cheat sheet | Task | Command or file | Guards against | |---|---|---| | Scaffold a compendium | `rrtools::use_compendium()`, `use_analysis()` | An improvised layout | | Pin the packages | `renv::init()`, `renv::snapshot()` | Newer packages on a collaborator's machine | | Pin what is beneath R | The canonical Dockerfile (@sec-docker-canonical) | A different R or system library | | Protect raw data | `MANIFEST.md5`; `md5sum -c MANIFEST.md5` | Edits saved over the raw export | | Audit the pillars | `audit_pillars('.')`; `git ls-files` | A pillar present on disk but not committed | | Render the paper | `quarto render analysis/paper/paper.qmd` | Typed numbers | | Use a journal format | `quarto use template quarto-journals/` | Reformatting by hand | | Test the compendium | Fresh clone, `docker build`, `docker run` | Files that live only on your machine | | Mark a milestone | `git tag -a v1.0-submission` | Not knowing what was submitted | : Compendium tasks at a glance. {#tbl-rrtools-cheat-sheet} ## Further reading - [@marwick2018packaging], the paper that defines the research compendium as this chapter uses it. - [@marwick2018rrtools], the `rrtools` package and its documentation. - [@harrell2025rworkflow], the closest peer treatment of what goes in the compendium's `analysis/` directory once it exists. ## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-07} 1. A research compendium is a directory tree that bundles a study's code, data, and narrative in one place, with a standardized layout. The reader can rerun the analyses and regenerate the paper with a single command. Marwick et al. (2018) argue that the compendium is the appropriate unit of reproducible research in R. 2. An R package backbone (`DESCRIPTION`, `R/`), an `analysis/` directory for data and the paper, and a Dockerfile for the computing environment. The package backbone gives dependency declaration (`Imports:`); the `analysis/` directory holds the study; the Dockerfile, with `renv.lock`, gives environment reproducibility. Together they make the compendium self-contained. 3. A regular R package exports functions for reuse by others; it has no data or narrative. An `rrtools` compendium adds `analysis/` (data and paper) and a Dockerfile, turning the package into a self-contained study with its own paper. The package structure is repurposed as infrastructure, not for distribution on CRAN.
